## Introduction

This micro case study uses simulated individual-level data to illustrate
the evaluation of a job training program.
The focus is on treatment effects, starting from descriptive analysis and
moving toward causal estimators in later sections.

## Data

The dataset is stored relative to the project root to ensure reproducibility.

```{r load-data}
case3A <- readRDS("data/micro/case3A_simulated.rds")
str(case3A)
```

## Descriptive Statistics

```{r summary}
summary(case3A)
```

## Treatment Assignment

```{r treatment}
table(case3A$treat)
```

## Outcome Variable

```{r outcome}
summary(case3A$y)
```

## Notes on Reproducibility

- All paths are relative to the project root.

- This file is intended to be rendered as part of a Quarto book.

## Difference in Means

The simplest estimator of the treatment effect compares mean outcomes
between treated and untreated individuals.

Formally, the difference-in-means estimator is:

$$
E[y \mid D = 1] - E[y \mid D = 0]
$$

This estimator does not control for selection into treatment and may therefore
be biased if treatment status is correlated with unobserved ability.

```{r diff-in-means}
mean_treated   <- mean(case3A$y[case3A$treat == 1])
mean_untreated <- mean(case3A$y[case3A$treat == 0])

diff_means <- mean_treated - mean_untreated

c(
  mean_treated   = mean_treated,
  mean_untreated = mean_untreated,
  diff_in_means  = diff_means
)
```

The estimated difference in means captures both the causal effect of the program
and any pre-existing differences between treated and untreated individuals.

## OLS Without Controls

The difference-in-means estimator can be written as a regression coefficient.
Consider the linear model:

$$
y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + u_i
$$

where $D_i$ is an indicator for participation in the job training program.

In this specification, the OLS estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is numerically identical
to the difference in mean outcomes between treated and untreated individuals.

```{r ols-no-controls}
ols_nc <- lm(y ~ treat, data = case3A)
summary(ols_nc)
```

To verify the equivalence with the difference-in-means estimator:

```{r ols-vs-dim}
coef(ols_nc)["treat"]
```

The estimated coefficient on the treatment indicator coincides with the
difference-in-means estimate reported in the previous section.

## OLS With Controls (Ability)

The previous specification ignores differences in individual ability.
If ability affects both program participation and labor market outcomes,
the estimated treatment effect will be biased.

To account for selection on ability, consider the following model:

$$
y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + \gamma \text{ability}_i + u_i
$$

```{r ols-with-ability}
ols_ability <- lm(y ~ treat + ability, data = case3A)
summary(ols_ability)
```

The inclusion of ability as a control variable reduces the estimated effect
of the training program relative to the unadjusted OLS specification.

This change reflects the fact that higher-ability individuals are both more
likely to participate in the program and to earn higher wages even in the
absence of treatment.

## True ATE vs Estimated Effects

Because the data are simulated, we observe potential outcomes for each individual.
This allows us to compute the true average treatment effect (ATE) directly.

The true ATE is defined as:

$$
ATE = E[y_1 - y_0]
$$

```{r true-ate}
true_ate <- mean(case3A$y1 - case3A$y0)
true_ate
```

We now compare the true ATE to previously estimated treatment effects.

```{r ate-comparison}
c(
  true_ate        = true_ate,
  diff_in_means   = diff_means,
  ols_no_controls = coef(ols_nc)["treat"],
  ols_with_ability = coef(ols_ability)["treat"]
)
```

The difference-in-means and unadjusted OLS estimates substantially overstate
the true causal effect due to positive selection into treatment.

Including ability as a control variable yields an estimate much closer to
the true ATE.

## Instrumental Variables

In many empirical applications, relevant control variables such as ability are
unobserved. In such cases, ordinary least squares estimation remains biased.

An alternative identification strategy relies on instrumental variables.
An instrument affects treatment participation but has no direct effect on the outcome.

In this simulation, the variable $z$ serves as an instrument for program participation.

### First Stage

The first-stage regression relates treatment participation to the instrument:

$$
D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_1 z_i + v_i
$$

```{r iv-first-stage}
first_stage <- lm(treat ~ z, data = case3A)
summary(first_stage)
```

### Reduced Form

The reduced form captures the effect of the instrument on the outcome:

```{r iv-reduced-form}
reduced_form <- lm(y ~ z, data = case3A)
summary(reduced_form)
```

### IV Estimation

The IV estimator can also be computed manually using a consistent definition
of the endogenous treatment variable.

```{r iv-manual-correct}
# Wald / IV estimator (self-contained)
fs_iv <- lm(treat_iv ~ z, data = case3A)
rf_iv <- lm(y ~ z, data = case3A)

iv_manual <- coef(rf_iv)["z"] / coef(fs_iv)["z"]
iv_manual
```

Equivalently, the IV estimate can be obtained using two-stage least squares:

```{r iv-2sls}
iv_2sls <- lm(y ~ treat_iv, data = case3A)
summary(iv_2sls)
```

The manual IV estimate coincides with the two-stage least squares result.
This highlights the importance of using a consistent endogenous variable
when applying the Wald formula.

The IV estimator can be computed as the ratio of the reduced-form and first-stage coefficients.


### Comparison with True ATE

```{r iv-vs-ate}
c(
  true_ate = true_ate,
  iv_estimate = coef(iv_2sls)["treat_iv"]
)
```

The IV estimate recovers the true causal effect of the training program
despite the presence of unobserved ability.


## Graphical Illustration of Bias

The figure below compares different estimators of the treatment effect
to the true average treatment effect (ATE).

```{r bias-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
# Collect estimates
estimates <- data.frame(
  estimator = c(
    "Difference in Means",
    "OLS (No Controls)",
    "OLS (Ability Control)",
    "IV / 2SLS"
  ),
  estimate = c(
    diff_means,
    coef(ols_nc)["treat"],
    coef(ols_ability)["treat"],
    coef(iv_2sls)["treat_iv"]
  )
)

# True ATE
true_ate_value <- true_ate

# Margins for rotated labels
op <- par(mar = c(9.5, 4, 2, 2))

plot(
  estimates$estimate,
  pch = 19,
  xaxt = "n",
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Estimated Treatment Effect",
  ylim = range(c(estimates$estimate, true_ate_value)) + c(-0.9, 0.3)
)

axis(
  1,
  at = seq_along(estimates$estimator),
  labels = estimates$estimator,
  las = 2,
  cex.axis = 0.85
)

abline(h = true_ate_value, lty = 2, col = "red")

text(
  x = seq_along(estimates$estimator),
  y = estimates$estimate,
  labels = round(estimates$estimate, 2),
  pos = 3, cex = 0.8
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = "True ATE",
  lty = 2, col = "red", bty = "n"
)

par(op)
```

The figure highlights how naive estimators overstate the true causal effect
due to selection bias, while instrumental variables recover the correct magnitude.
The figure highlights how naive estimators overstate the true causal effect due to selection bias, while instrumental variables recover the correct magnitude.

This case study illustrates how different empirical strategies identify
very different estimates of the same treatment effect.

Simple comparisons of mean outcomes and unadjusted OLS substantially overstate
the true effect of the job training program due to positive selection into treatment.

Controlling for individual ability greatly reduces this bias, but such controls
are rarely observed in real-world data.

Instrumental variables provide a powerful alternative identification strategy
when relevant confounders are unobserved.

In this simulation, the IV estimator successfully recovers the true average
treatment effect, highlighting the importance of credible instruments in
causal inference.

## Conclusion

very different estimates of the same treatment effect.

Simple comparisons of mean outcomes and unadjusted OLS substantially overstate
the true effect of the job training program due to positive selection into treatment.

Controlling for individual ability greatly reduces this bias, but such controls
are rarely observed in real-world data.

Instrumental variables provide a powerful alternative identification strategy
when relevant confounders are unobserved.

In this simulation, the IV estimator successfully recovers the true average
treatment effect, highlighting the importance of credible instruments in
causal inference.
